> Unfortunately, `StringName::_Data` cannot be fully localized because the pointer of existing `StringName` instances must not be invalidated.

Speaking of this, I think `PagedArray`(`core/templates/paged_array.h`) may be relevant. Happened to come across it today and based on its description it won't move its elements.

> Speaking of this, I think PagedArray(core/templates/paged_array.h) may be relevant. Happened to come across it today and based on its description it won't move its elements.

Yeah, I can imagine `PagedArray` could help performance further. Perhaps we could take a look at that some time too!

> Maybe it would be worth tinkering with the buckets size, the whole 16bits, aka 65k buckets seems a lot, but hard to tell without data.

Agreed. Big buckets were a bottleneck before this PR, but since that's now alleviated we can definitely rethink the bucket sizes.

Could you try including removing Nodes from the tree in your c++ benchmark?  I tried benchmarking in gdscript with the below - smaller difference is expected with the gdscript overhead, but what seems odd is the removal is consistently slower for me.  I'm wondering how much of the difference comes from using `LocalVector::push_back()` to add new data to the end, while before new data was added to the beginning of the list.

I think there's two main ways StringNames are involved when creating new Nodes.  When new nodes are added to the tree, they get a unique name assigned if they don't already have one.  When adding a ton of Nodes to the tree at the same time, it basically floods the StringName table with these unique names, resulting in the lists/LocalVectors becoming longer.  There's also the StringNames from the GDVIRTUAL macros on Node - "_process", "_physics_process", etc.  These are created (looked up, not reallocated) for each created Node, even though they all have the same value (maybe these could be static in the future?).  Before, since the node names were added to the beginning of the lists, the macro strings kept getting pushed back, making them take longer to look up on node creation.  Now that the macro strings stay at the beginning, they're found faster, and Node creation is faster.  But that would also mean the node names are further back in the LocalVector, so freeing nodes and deleting the name string has to look further and takes longer.

In gdscript at least, the add speeds up by more than the remove slows down for large numbers of nodes, so the tradeoff seems to be worth it, but would be good to get a better idea what's happening on the c++ side.

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	test_add_remove(50000)
	test_add_remove(500000)
	test_add_remove(1000000)

func test_add_remove(p_count : int):
	var start := Time.get_ticks_msec()
	for i in p_count:
		add_child(Node.new())
	var end := Time.get_ticks_msec()
	print("%s %d: %dms" % ["add", p_count, end - start])
	start = Time.get_ticks_msec()
	for child in get_children():
		child.free()
	end = Time.get_ticks_msec()
	print("%s %d: %dms" % ["rem", p_count, end - start])
```

> Some difference is to be expected, because removing from the list when you have the element pointer requires only 2 or 3 dereferences, while removing from LocalVector requires that but also searching for the entry first.


That makes sense!  I was thinking of both versions looping through in `unref` after looking at the new code, but the old code didn't have that loop.  Might be something to watch out for if we end up reducing the number of buckets.  Also, maybe it would be possible to store the LocalVector index in _data (if we can keep it updated after `remove_at_unordered`), so it could jump straight there?  That sounds like it might add an extra pointer to follow for each delete though, not sure if it'd actually help.

I was testing with ef1153baf and the changes applied from there.  It varies a bit from run to run, but I think the percentage differences are similar for the larger set, maybe a bit smaller for going through gdscript.  Overall, even with removes being slower, the combined add+remove definitely seems to scale up better with this change.

> LocalVector index in _data (if we can keep it updated after remove_at_unordered)

I was about to say that would cost as much as it brings, but with remove_at_unordered we would actually only have to update a single Data's value! I'll test that.

@aaronp64 Your suggestion works great! Caching the entry's index so removing entries does not need to search the array seems to eliminate most measurable 'removal' differences for me.

I've once again run some tests, this time with a bit more sophistication with different amounts of `StringName`:
<details>
<summary>Test Code</summary>

```c++
	size_t N = 20000000;
	for (size_t array_size : { 1, 8, 64, 1000, 10000, 100000, 1000000 }) {
		{
			size_t total_ns = 0;
			for (size_t j = 0; j < N / array_size; ++j) {
				LocalVector<StringName> names;
				names.resize(array_size);

				auto t0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
				for (size_t i = 0; i < array_size; i ++) {
					names[i] = StringName(String::num_int64(i));
				}
				auto t1 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
				total_ns += std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(t1 - t0).count();
			}

			std::cout << "construct " << array_size << std::endl;
			std::cout << total_ns / 1000 / 1000 << "ms\n";
		}
		{
			size_t total_ns = 0;
			for (size_t j = 0; j < N / array_size; ++j) {
				LocalVector<StringName> names;
				names.resize(array_size);

				for (size_t i = 0; i < array_size; i ++) {
					names[i] = StringName(String::num_int64(i));
				}
				auto t0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
				for (size_t i = 0; i < array_size; i ++) {
					names[i] = StringName();
				}
				auto t1 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
				total_ns += std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(t1 - t0).count();
			}

			std::cout << "destruct " << array_size << std::endl;
			std::cout << total_ns / 1000 / 1000 << "ms\n";
		}
	}
```
</details>

In short, I've found that this PR is still better than `master` across the board, though not as much as before my other optimizations:
- `1 StringName:` ~same
- `8 StringName:` 2% worse
- `64 StringName:` 4% better
- `1000 StringName:` 4% better
- `10000 StringName:` 6% better
- `100000 StringName:` 5% better
- `1000000 StringName:` 12% better

The differences are way worse if i decrease the number of buckets (this PR with 2^14 buckets, compared to master):
- `1 StringName:` ~same
- `8 StringName:` 2% worse
- `64 StringName:` 1% worse
- `1000 StringName:` 70% worse
- `10000 StringName:` 8% worse
- `100000 StringName:` 7% worse
- `1000000 StringName:` 3% better

At this point, I'm not sure if this PR is still worth it. The improvement isn't _nothing_, but it's also not all that exciting, considering most games will probably stay in the ~5% range. Considering it's somewhat of a risk to change the implementation in such a drastic way, it may be more interesting to explore another approach entirely.
(this conclusion comes with the caveat that these are benchmarks, and this may affect actual programs differently due to cache contention)

For anyone that's been following this PR, do not fret - my previous PRs have already sped up `StringName` significantly, so we should already be seeing most of the benefits proclaimed here initially :)
